result:
I want to write about the strange intimacy of watching someone choose fruit at the grocery store. There's something about this mundane ritual that feels almost voyeuristic when you really pay attention. The way a person will press a thumb gently against an avocado's skin, searching for that perfect give. The deliberation over a bunch of bananas—counting, estimating, calculating days of ripeness against their own eating schedule. Do they live alone? Will these brown before they can finish them? 

I think we reveal ourselves in these small economies. The woman who inspects every apple before committing, turning each one like a jeweler with a gem. The man who grabs the first three oranges he touches, confident or careless or simply exhausted. The elderly person who takes forever with the pears, not because they're picky but because this is a moment of sensory engagement in a day that might otherwise feel empty.

I've noticed I buy more fragile produce when I'm lonely. Raspberries, figs, delicate things that demand my attention, that force me to eat them before they surrender to time. It's a strange self-care, choosing something that will spoil if I don't tend to it. A small, perishable companion.

The grocery store fluorescent lights make everyone look slightly unwell, but in the produce section, there's this weird tenderness. People touching living things, however briefly, before the things become food, become consumed, become part of the ongoing project of staying alive for one more day.
